finding.claim: Broken authorization: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result instead of using require_edit(), so any caller can overwrite any document's body regardless of ownership/editor status.
finding.source: Any authenticated (or any request-context) user sending PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON {"body": ...}; doc_id is attacker-chosen
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20 (write to the document store)

trace.note: doc = DOCS[doc_id] looked up with no ownership check
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns False for non-editors but return value is ignored; no abort(403)

finding.guards_checked: Compared with update_title (line 27) which correctly uses require_edit() that aborts 403. No before_request/auth decorator exists in the file; g.user is never set here, so authentication is presumably elsewhere and, even if present, there is no per-document authorization. The can_edit result is not used.

verdict.guard_found: can_edit() at docs.py:7-8 returns a bool, but update_doc discards it at line 19; require_edit() (docs.py:11-13, which aborts 403) is only used in update_title. No before_request or decorator exists in the file.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) as a bare statement with the result discarded, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any user who can reach the route, unlike update_title, which calls require_edit at docs.py:27.
